clue.text: Loses hope as spa dries.

blocks.note: the two words supply all eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A spa owner gives up as the waters of the resort run dry.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram indicator here: the setter lets the two words after 'as' be rearranged on their own, so the solver must spot that they have exactly eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To give up all expectation of something improving is the plain meaning of this verb, in the same third person singular form.

clue.text: Adorn a device for measuring up to 11 yards?

definitions.note: a cryptic hint at the length rather than a synonym

blocks.note: to deck is to adorn or decorate
taken as written
a meter is a measuring instrument, spelt here as the unit

explanation.surface: Someone decorates a gadget that measures distances of about eleven yards.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, the answer is 'deck a meter', which is 'adorn a device for measuring'; there is no separate sound signal, the question mark carries it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten metres comes to about 10.9 yards, so the unit measures just under eleven yards, hence the hedging question mark.

clue.text: Step one in celestial body.

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside the other word's letters

blocks.note: a star is a heavenly body
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Taking a first step on to a planet or star, like an astronaut.
explanation.walkthrough: The I goes inside STAR, between the T and the R, giving STAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A single tread of a staircase is a step, so the two nouns are direct synonyms.

clue.text: Sounds like the ideal accompaniment to a sneeze.

indicators.note: these words tell us to go by how a phrase is pronounced, not how it is written

blocks.note: the perfect thing to have with a sneeze is a handkerchief or paper hanky

explanation.surface: A light remark that the best companion for a sneeze is some noise or a hanky.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'accompaniment to a sneeze' does double duty: the ideal one is a tissue, and the noise that goes with it is the answer, which sounds like 'a tissue'.
explanation.definitionFit: The conventional written form of the noise a person makes when sneezing, which comes with the sneeze itself.

clue.text: Referring to or concerning a period of brutal oppression.

indicators.note: something concerning is troubling, so the preceding words are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: all thirteen letters of these three words are used

explanation.surface: It reads like a history textbook's introduction to a chapter on a tyrannical era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Referring to or concerning' looks like a dull phrase of academic prose; the first three words are the fodder and 'concerning' stirs them up.
explanation.definitionFit: The name was first given to the bloody phase of the French Revolution under Robespierre and now covers any era of savage repression.

clue.text: Partially risk a terrible injury on the ice.

definitions.note: a phrase describing the person rather than a noun

indicators.note: only part of the following run of words is used, so the letters lie within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the middle word and the start of the third
surface padding that makes the ice sound dangerous

explanation.surface: A warning that you take a chance of nasty harm when you go out on the ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injury' is surface padding that lets 'on the ice' read as a place where people get hurt; the definition is the one found on the ice.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone gliding over a rink or frozen pond is the person found out on the ice, a loose descriptive definition.

clue.text: Lacking dominion in part. Not in this realm.

indicators.note: only a portion of the preceding words is wanted, so the answer is tucked inside them

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone without any power or authority in a land that is not theirs to rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a country ruled by a monarch, the same thing as a state headed by a king or queen.

clue.text: Bitter charges for acidic salts.

blocks.note: sharp or sour in taste
rates are fees or prices charged

explanation.surface: Resentful complaints about the fees paid for some chemicals.
explanation.definitionFit: These are compounds formed from tartaric acid, the salts or esters of that acid, as in cream of tartar.

clue.text: Depend on it, only without me.

indicators.note: going without something means it is removed and left out

blocks.note: a synonym meaning just or simply
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wry reassurance: you can count on it, provided I am not involved.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking ME from the front of MERELY leaves RELY. 'Depend on it' reads as a set phrase, but only 'Depend' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To trust in someone or something for support is to count upon it, so both verbs share that sense.

clue.text: Endless confused action for raccoon.

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter of the word is removed
something confused is muddled, so the letters are jumbled up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Chaotic activity laid on to catch or entertain a raccoon.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the last N leaves ACTIO, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-snouted South American mammal belongs to the raccoon family, so it is a raccoon in the broad zoological sense.

clue.text: E-learning astray, by and large.

indicators.note: letters that have gone astray have wandered out of their proper order

blocks.note: all nine letters, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: Online study usually goes off course, so it is said.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are adverbial idioms meaning on the whole, taking everything into account, mostly.

clue.text: Nerve centre for land management.

blocks.note: land or earth
running or direction of something

explanation.surface: An office that serves as the headquarters for managing an estate.
explanation.definitionFit: The station on Earth that directs a space flight or aircraft is its command hub, the heart of operations.

clue.text: E.g. "Best foot forward", given on dismissal.

definitions.note: an example of one such command, while the answer is plural

blocks.note: first meaning: commands given to troops on the move
second meaning: notice that someone is sacked or sent away

explanation.surface: An upbeat motto handed to someone as they are fired from their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best foot forward' is an encouraging saying, but read literally it is an instruction for setting off on a march.
explanation.definitionFit: Orders to set off on a march are literally this, and being given them figuratively means being told to leave a job or relationship.

clue.text: Accomplish easily, and dispense with the pre-match routine

blocks.note: first meaning: produce something quickly with little effort
second meaning: the coin flip before a game is called off

explanation.surface: A captain who finds the game easy and skips the formalities before kick-off.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is whimsical: if the coin flip that starts a match is cancelled, the toss is off.
explanation.definitionFit: To dash something off without effort is a common phrasal verb, and read literally it also cancels the coin flip.

clue.text: Foreign miss by design or inadvertently.

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word, through the second, into the third

explanation.surface: Whether deliberately or by accident, someone from abroad goes astray.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate concealment signal; the phrase 'by design or inadvertently' reads naturally while hiding the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Italian title for an unmarried young woman, the equivalent of the English title Miss.

clue.text: Gate man verifies one's identity.

definitions.note: describes what the thing does rather than naming it

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A doorman checks who someone is before letting them in.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no direction signal: the two words simply read right to left give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A badge pinned on at a conference shows the wearer's name, telling others who that person is.

clue.text: Convenience for adult males.

blocks.note: first meaning: a public toilet, from the sign on the door
second meaning: grown men, politely put

explanation.surface: It reads like a sign announcing a toilet for men only.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'convenience' is the British euphemism for a public lavatory, and the men's one is labelled with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word on the door of a men's public toilet names the facility, and it is also a courteous plural for grown men.

clue.text: Opening position heard to be vigilant

indicators.note: something heard is taken in by ear, so pronunciation matters here

blocks.note: being on the lookout for danger

explanation.surface: A newcomer told that a starting job demands constant alertness.
explanation.walkthrough: The French fencing call is roughly pronounced like the English phrase for watchful.
explanation.definitionFit: In fencing this is the ready stance taken at the start of a bout, the first position before attacking.

clue.text: Disproves arbiter set up around university.

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the word from bottom to top
one part is placed around another so it sits inside

blocks.note: short for referee, the arbiter of a game
taken as written
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A judge of the facts shows a claim to be false while sitting on a campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' reads as a verb phrase meaning framed, but in this down clue 'set' is simply turned upwards; U then slips between the referee and that word.
explanation.definitionFit: To refute an argument is to show it to be false, so the verbs match exactly in sense and tense.

clue.text: Roughen no cares.

blocks.note: all seven letters are used

explanation.surface: A carefree attitude, telegraphically linked to getting rough.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal at all; the two words have exactly the letters needed and must be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a surface or texture less smooth, or manners cruder, is both to roughen and to make coarse.

clue.text: Mean to state how old one is.

blocks.note: to aver is to declare or assert
the number of years one has lived

explanation.surface: Someone intends to reveal their age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like the verb 'intend', but it is the statistical noun.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics the arithmetic mean of a set of figures is their sum divided by the count, the usual average.

clue.text: Telephone meeting to discuss pear name?

blocks.note: first meaning: a phone call linking several people
second meaning, whimsical: what you call one popular variety of pear

explanation.surface: Arranging a phone meeting to talk about what to name a pear.
explanation.walkthrough: Conference is a well-known British pear variety, so to call a pear by that name is a Conference call.
explanation.definitionFit: A phone call where several parties join in at once is a standard business term, and a call is also a name given.

clue.text: Friend to a damaged imago.

indicators.note: something damaged is broken up, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone befriends an adult insect whose wings have been hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: An imago is an insect in its final adult form, such as a butterfly emerged from its chrysalis.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Spanish word for a pal, widely borrowed into informal English for a close companion.

clue.text: Daughter leaves new wife for cheese.

indicators.note: when one thing leaves, it departs and is no longer present in the word

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation
a woman just married

explanation.surface: A daughter walks out on her father's new bride and makes do with cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the D out of BRIDE leaves BRIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft French variety with a white rind, from the region east of Paris, is one kind of the dairy food.

clue.text: Terrorise madly a noisy reveller.

indicators.note: acting madly means wildly and without order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: all nine letters are used

explanation.surface: A rowdy partygoer frightens everyone in a wild way.
explanation.definitionFit: To roister is to celebrate boisterously, so someone who does it is a loud merrymaker.

clue.text: Terminate island dependency: that's self-evident.

blocks.note: to axe is to end, in its American spelling
the Isle of Man, a self-governing Crown dependency

explanation.surface: A call to end the island's reliance on Britain, presented as obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland, is not part of the UK but a Crown dependency, abbreviated IOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement accepted as true without proof, needing no demonstration, is the basis of logic and mathematics.

clue.text: Pass by eastern failing.

blocks.note: the compass abbreviation
a slip or a lapse of standards

explanation.surface: Something from the east goes by and then breaks down.
explanation.definitionFit: When time goes on and is gone, it slips away or passes, the sense of the verb.

clue.text: Rare occurrence of a depressed satellite.

blocks.note: feeling down or sad
a natural body orbiting a planet

explanation.surface: It is unusual to find an orbiting body that feels gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'once in a ...' means very seldom.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens extremely seldom is said to happen once in this, after the occasional second full moon in a month.
